## Abstract
Long-running RAG services incur a hidden systems cost: retrieval remains active even when the memory it accesses has become stale, cold, or redundant. We present a resource-aware memory lifecycle management framework for long-term RAG inference with compact language models, and evaluate its computational efficiency on a combined 664-problem code generation benchmark under simulated long-term deployment conditions. Using an Ebbinghaus-inspired memory state machine with five states, we track simulated memory evolution across four compact models---Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Phi-3-mini-4k, Gemma-2-2B, and a seven-round distilled Qwen2.5-3B variant---quantized to GGUF Q4_K_M for efficient CPU/GPU inference via llama.cpp. Three main observations emerge: (1)~~in simulated 90-day deployment under power-law access, active retrieval memory reaches complete depletion (100% active-memory depletion) by day~~ 30 across all tested architectures, yet the distilled model maintains stable Pass@1 ($0.093$ at $t{=}0$d vs.$0.102$ at $t{=}90$d), suggesting that, for the distilled model after memory convergence, retrieval can be disabled without degrading Pass@1 in our setting---yielding a 25.8% inference time reduction (1038s vs.\1398s for full RAG on 664 problems; per-query: 1.56s vs.\2.11s) and approximately 10.2% per-query latency savings on the 34-problem diagnostic set (1.37s vs.\1.51s); (2)~as a consistency check, lifecycle entropy under the shared memory policy follows a near-identical three-phase trajectory across all four models (standard deviation $0.017$ at peak), confirming that the memory state machine design, not the downstream model, governs the observed lifecycle dynamics; (3)~retrieval usefulness is near zero in the distilled model ($0.005$--$0.018$), and a memory-priority inference strategy recovers No-RAG performance, further reducing unnecessary retrieval computation. These results, obtained under simulated access patterns, suggest that lifecycle-aware retrieval scheduling can provide measurable computational savings in long-term RAG deployments, and that for sufficiently distilled compact models, periodic retrieval deactivation represents a practical resource optimization strategy warranting validation on real-world deployment traces.
